lesson.title: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
objectives: Explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a rendered page.
Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response: method, path, headers, body and status code.
Distinguish safe and idempotent HTTP methods and explain why the difference matters for retries.
Group status codes into their five classes and choose the right one for common situations.
Parse a raw HTTP request in JavaScript.
lesson.definition: The web is a client-server system: a client such as a browser sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server returns an HTTP response. HTTP is a stateless, text-based application protocol (binary-framed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) that runs over TCP or QUIC, usually wrapped in TLS as HTTPS. DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the IP address the client connects to.

theory.heading: From URL to page
theory.body: When a user opens https://codinghub.in/courses, the browser first resolves the domain to an IP address through DNS (checking its own cache, the operating system, then a recursive resolver). It opens a TCP connection (or a QUIC connection for HTTP/3), performs a TLS handshake to encrypt the channel and verify the server's certificate, and sends an HTTP request. The server returns HTML, the browser parses it, discovers CSS, JavaScript and images, and fetches those with further requests before rendering.
points: DNS: domain name to IP address, cached according to its TTL.
TCP/QUIC: a reliable connection to the server's IP and port (443 for HTTPS).
TLS: encryption plus certificate-based server identity.
HTTP: the request/response exchange itself.
Rendering: HTML parsed into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM, then layout and paint.

theory.heading: Anatomy of a request and a response
theory.body: A request has a method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), a target path with an optional query string, headers (metadata such as Host, Content-Type, Authorization, Cookie) and an optional body. A response has a status code, headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie) and a body. Headers are case-insensitive; the Host header lets one IP address serve many domains.
points: Request line: METHOD /path?query HTTP/1.1
Headers: Name: value, one per line, ended by a blank line.
Body: JSON, form data or a file; its type is declared in Content-Type.
Response: status line, headers, blank line, body.

theory.heading: Methods: safe and idempotent
theory.body: A safe method does not change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). An idempotent method has the same effect whether it is sent once or many times (the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE). POST is neither, which is why a network retry of a POST can create two orders or charge a card twice. Clients and proxies retry idempotent requests automatically; for POST you need an idempotency key or deduplication on the server.
points: GET reads, POST creates or triggers actions, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.
Idempotent does not mean the same response: a second DELETE may return 404, but the state is the same.
Calling an LLM endpoint is usually a POST, so retries must be designed deliberately.

theory.heading: Status code classes
theory.body: Status codes tell the client what happened without parsing the body. 1xx is informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a client error the client should fix, and 5xx a server error the client may retry later. Using precise codes lets front ends, monitoring and load balancers behave correctly.
points: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.
301/308 permanent redirect, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified (cache still valid).
400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthenticated, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 validation failed, 429 Too Many Requests.
500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout.

theory.heading: Statelessness, cookies and the AI web app
theory.body: HTTP itself remembers nothing between requests, so state is carried explicitly: cookies, tokens in the Authorization header, or IDs in the URL. A typical AI web app has a React client, an API server that holds secrets and talks to the database and the LLM provider, and a CDN for static files. Understanding this request flow is the base for later topics such as streaming, authentication and rate limiting.
points: Stateless servers scale horizontally: any instance can handle any request.
The browser never calls the LLM provider directly with a secret key; the back end does.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP).

example.title: A chat request and its response
example.body: The React front end sends the user's message to its own back end. The POST carries JSON and a bearer token. The server answers 201 with JSON. Notice the blank line separating headers from the body and the Content-Type header describing the body format.

POST /api/chats/17/messages HTTP/1.1
Host: app.codinghub.in
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

{"content": "Explain closures in JavaScript"}

Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 90, "role": "user", "content": "Explain closures in JavaScript"}

use_cases.title: Designing safe retries
use_cases.description: Knowing which methods are idempotent tells you which failed calls a client can repeat automatically and which need idempotency keys.

use_cases.title: Error handling in the UI

demonstration.description: Use fetch from the browser console to call a public JSON endpoint and inspect the parts of the response. The status, headers and body are separate pieces of the HTTP message.
demonstration.output:
200 true
application/json; charset=utf-8
delectus aut autem

takeaways: DNS resolves the name, TCP/QUIC connects, TLS secures, HTTP exchanges the request and response.
A request is method + target + headers + optional body; a response is status + headers + body.
Safe methods do not change state; idempotent methods can be repeated with the same effect.
POST is not idempotent, so retries need an idempotency key or server-side deduplication.
4xx means the client must change something; 5xx means the server failed and a retry may succeed.
HTTP is stateless; cookies and tokens carry identity between requests.

interview.question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
interview.answer: The browser parses the URL, resolves the domain through DNS, opens a TCP (or QUIC) connection, performs a TLS handshake for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, then parses HTML, fetches sub-resources (CSS, JS, images) and renders the page.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want the ordered chain, not every detail. Mention caching at each layer (DNS cache, HTTP cache) and that rendering involves the DOM and CSSOM for extra credit.

interview.question: What is the difference between GET and POST?
interview.answer: GET retrieves a resource, is safe and idempotent, sends parameters in the URL and can be cached and bookmarked. POST submits data in the body to create something or trigger an action; it is neither safe nor idempotent and is not cached by default.
interview.explanation: Avoid saying POST is 'more secure': both are visible to anyone without HTTPS. The real difference is semantics, idempotency and caching.

interview.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
interview.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the request is not authenticated: credentials are missing or invalid. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you lack permission for this resource.
interview.explanation: A strong answer adds the UI consequence: on 401 redirect to login or refresh the token; on 403 show an access-denied message, because logging in again will not help.

interview.question: What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter for an API that calls an LLM?
interview.answer: An idempotent operation produces the same server state whether it runs once or many times. LLM calls are usually POSTs that cost money and may create records, so blind retries can double charges or duplicate messages. Use idempotency keys or deduplicate on the server before retrying.
interview.explanation: Linking HTTP semantics to cost and duplicate data shows you think about production behaviour, not just definitions.

interview.question: Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do web apps keep users logged in?
interview.answer: Each request is independent and the server keeps no built-in memory of earlier requests. Apps carry state explicitly: a session ID in a cookie that maps to server-side data, or a signed token (such as a JWT) sent on every request.
interview.explanation: Mention that statelessness is what allows horizontal scaling behind a load balancer, which leads naturally into session storage choices (Day 14).

interview.question: What changed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
interview.answer: HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexes many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, with header compression. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, which removes TCP head-of-line blocking and makes connection setup faster, especially on mobile networks.
interview.explanation: You do not need protocol internals; showing why multiplexing helps pages with many assets is enough.

practice.title: Parse a raw HTTP request
practice.objective: Read the parts of an HTTP request the way a server framework does, and classify the method as safe and/or idempotent.
practice.statement: The input is a raw HTTP/1.1 request: a request line, header lines until a blank line, and an optional body. Print the method, the path without the query string, the decoded query parameters, the Host header and whether the method is safe and idempotent. Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent methods: the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE.
practice.input_format: Line 1: METHOD TARGET HTTP/1.1. Then zero or more 'Name: value' header lines, a blank line, and an optional body (ignored).
practice.output_format:
Six lines:
Method: <method>
Path: <path>
Query: <k=v; k=v> in original order, or 'none'
Host: <host header value> or 'missing'
Safe: yes|no
Idempotent: yes|no

example.input:
GET /api/courses?page=2&q=ai+tools HTTP/1.1
Host: codinghub.in
Accept: application/json
example.output:
Method: GET
Path: /api/courses
Query: page=2; q=ai tools
Host: codinghub.in
Safe: yes
Idempotent: yes

constraints: Header names are case-insensitive (host, Host and HOST are the same header).
Query keys and values are URL-decoded; '+' means a space.
A parameter without '=' has an empty value (print 'key=').
explanation: Split the input into lines; the first line holds the method and the request target.
Read headers until the first blank line, storing names in lowercase so lookups are case-insensitive.
Split the target at the first '?' into path and query string.
Split the query on '&', split each pair at the first '=', and URL-decode both sides after turning '+' into spaces.
Classify the method with two small lists: safe methods, and idempotent methods (safe plus PUT and DELETE).

quiz.question: What is the job of DNS when a browser opens a website?
options: Translating a domain name into an IP address
Encrypting traffic between browser and server
quiz.explanation: DNS maps names such as codinghub.in to IP addresses. Encryption is TLS's job and rendering is the browser engine's.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is idempotent but NOT safe?
quiz.explanation: PUT changes state (not safe) but repeating the same PUT leaves the same state (idempotent). GET and HEAD are both; POST is neither.

quiz.question: A logged-in student calls an admin-only endpoint. The server recognises the student's valid token. Which status code fits best?
quiz.explanation: The user is authenticated but not permitted, which is 403. 401 is for missing or invalid credentials.

quiz.question: A mobile client's POST /api/orders times out and the client retries automatically. Two orders appear. What is the most robust fix?
options: Send an idempotency key so the server can detect the duplicate
Increase the client timeout to five minutes
quiz.explanation: POST is not idempotent. An idempotency key lets the server return the first result for a repeated request instead of creating a duplicate.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
const res = new Response('{}', { status: 503 });
console.log(res.ok, Math.floor(res.status / 100));
quiz.explanation: res.ok is true only for 200–299, so it is false. Math.floor(503 / 100) gives the status class 5 (server error).

lesson.title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
objectives: Explain the differences between var, let and const, including hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
Define a closure and use one to keep private state.
Use destructuring, spread/rest, template literals, optional chaining and nullish coalescing correctly.
Transform data with map, filter, reduce and sort without mutating the source.
Explain how arrow functions treat this differently from regular functions.
lesson.definition: ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) and later versions added block-scoped variables, arrow functions, classes, modules, destructuring, spread syntax, promises and many array and object helpers to JavaScript. A closure is a function bundled with the variables of the scope it was created in, so it can read and update those variables even after the outer function has returned.

theory.heading: var, let and const
theory.body: var is function-scoped and hoisted with the value undefined, so it leaks out of blocks such as if and for. let and const are block-scoped; they are hoisted too, but reading them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError (the temporal dead zone). const prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the object it points to. Modern code uses const by default and let when the variable must be reassigned.
points: const user = {}; user.name = 'Asha' is allowed; user = {} is not.
for (let i ...) creates a fresh i per iteration; for (var i ...) shares one i.
Avoid var in new code.

theory.heading: Closures
theory.body: Every function remembers the lexical environment where it was defined. When an inner function is returned or passed as a callback, it still has access to the outer variables. This is how JavaScript creates private state without classes, and it is the mechanism behind React hooks, event handlers, debounce utilities and module patterns. A classic bug is a stale closure: a callback captures an old value and keeps using it after the value has changed.
points: Private state: a counter factory exposes increment() but hides count.
Function factories: makeMultiplier(3) returns a function that multiplies by 3.
Stale closures appear in React effects and timers that capture old state.

theory.heading: Modern syntax you will use daily
theory.body: Destructuring pulls values out of objects and arrays; spread copies or merges them; rest collects remaining items. Optional chaining (a?.b) stops at null or undefined instead of throwing, and nullish coalescing (x ?? fallback) uses the fallback only for null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0, '' and false. These features are everywhere in React props and API response handling.
points: const { name, role = 'student' } = user; default applies only when the value is undefined.
const next = { ...state, count: state.count + 1 } makes a shallow copy.
res.data?.choices?.[0]?.message ?? 'No reply' guards a deeply nested API field.
Template literals: `Hello ${name}` with embedded expressions.

theory.heading: Array methods and immutability
theory.body: map transforms each item, filter keeps items that pass a test, reduce folds a list into one value, find returns the first match, and some/every test conditions. They return new values instead of modifying the input, which is exactly what React state updates require. Note that sort and reverse mutate the original array; use [...arr].sort() or the newer toSorted() to stay immutable.
points: map → same length, transformed items.
filter → same or fewer items, unchanged.
reduce(fn, initial) → any shape: a number, an object, a grouped map.
sort compares as strings by default: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9].

theory.heading: Arrow functions and this
theory.body: A regular function gets this from how it is called (obj.method() sets this to obj). An arrow function has no own this: it uses this from the surrounding scope. That makes arrows ideal for callbacks inside methods, but wrong as object methods that need the object as this. Arrows also have no arguments object and cannot be used with new.
points: Use arrows for callbacks: items.map((x) => x * 2).
Use regular methods when you need the object as this.

example.title: A closure-based usage tracker
example.body: This factory keeps a per-user token count private. Callers can add usage and read the total, but cannot change count directly because it only exists inside the closure.

use_cases.title: Shaping API responses
use_cases.description: map and filter turn a raw list of records into the exact props a React component needs.

use_cases.title: Aggregations in the browser
use_cases.description: reduce groups items by category or sums prices in a cart without a library.

use_cases.title: Encapsulated utilities
use_cases.description: Closures power debounce, throttle, memoize and per-user counters.

use_cases.title: Safe access to nested data
use_cases.description: Optional chaining and ?? handle missing fields in LLM or third-party API responses without crashes.

demonstration.description: Group chat messages by role and count tokens per role with one reduce call, then show that the input array was not modified.

takeaways: Prefer const, use let for reassignment, avoid var.
A closure keeps access to its outer variables; it enables private state and is behind React hooks.
?? falls back only for null/undefined; || also replaces 0, '' and false.
map, filter and reduce return new values; sort and reverse mutate unless you copy first.
Spread makes shallow copies: nested objects are still shared.
Arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope.

interview.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
interview.answer: var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined when hoisted. let and const are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until declared. const cannot be reassigned, though an object it holds can still be mutated.
interview.explanation: Mention the loop example (var shares one variable across iterations) and that const is about the binding, not deep immutability.

interview.question: What is a closure? Give a practical example.
interview.answer: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created. Example: a counter factory that returns increment and get functions sharing a private count, or a debounce function that remembers its timer ID between calls.
interview.explanation: A concrete use (private state, debounce, React hooks) is what separates a strong answer from a memorised definition.

interview.question: What does this print, and why? for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));
interview.answer: It prints 3, 3, 3. var creates one function-scoped i shared by all callbacks, and the callbacks run after the loop has finished. Changing var to let prints 0, 1, 2 because let creates a new binding per iteration.
interview.explanation: This classic question tests scope, closures and the event loop together. Explain both the cause and the fix.

interview.question: When would you use reduce instead of map or filter?
interview.answer: Use reduce when the result has a different shape from the input, for example a total, an object keyed by category, or a lookup map. Use map for one-to-one transforms and filter for selecting items, because they are clearer.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like hearing that readability matters: chaining filter then map is often clearer than one clever reduce.

interview.question: Is the spread operator a deep copy? Why does this matter in React?
interview.answer: No. Spread copies only the top level; nested objects and arrays are shared references. In React, mutating a nested object after spreading changes the old state too, which can cause missed re-renders or bugs. Copy every level you change, or use structuredClone or a helper like Immer.
interview.explanation: Connecting shallow copies to React's reference-equality checks shows you understand why immutability matters, not just the rule.

practice.title: Course leaderboard with map, filter and reduce
practice.objective: Practise the parse → validate → group → aggregate pipeline using array methods and immutable sorting.
practice.statement: Each input line is 'name,course,score'. A record is valid when name and course are non-empty and score is a number from 0 to 100. Group valid records by course and, for each course in alphabetical order, print the average score (one decimal place), the top student (highest score; ties go to the alphabetically first name) and the number of students. Finally print how many lines were skipped as invalid. If there are no valid records, print 'No valid records' before the skipped count.
practice.input_format: Zero or more non-empty lines 'name,course,score'. Surrounding spaces around each field are ignored.
practice.output_format: One line per course: '<course>: avg=<x.x> top=<name> (<score>) count=<n>', then 'Skipped: <k>'.

example.output:
node: avg=75.0 top=Kiran (75) count=2
react: avg=83.3 top=Ravi (92) count=3
Skipped: 0

constraints: Scores may be decimals; print them as JavaScript prints numbers (75, 99.5).
Course names are compared with plain string ordering.
Do not mutate the parsed array when sorting; copy it first.
explanation: Split into trimmed, non-empty lines and map each to an object with destructuring defaults for missing fields.
Convert the score with Number, treating an empty string as NaN so it fails validation.
filter keeps valid records; reduce groups them into an object keyed by course.
For each course (sorted keys), compute the average with reduce and find the top student by sorting a copy with a two-level comparator.
The skipped count is the difference between parsed and valid lengths.

tests.output:
node: avg=75.0 top=Kiran (75) count=2
react: avg=83.3 top=Ravi (92) count=3
Skipped: 0

ai: avg=99.5 top=Ira (99.5) count=1
python: avg=64.0 top=Neha (64) count=1
Skipped: 2

quiz.question: What does this code print?
quiz.explanation: let creates a new binding of i for each iteration, so each closure captures its own value.

quiz.question: What is logged?
quiz.explanation: || treats 0 as falsy and returns 10; ?? only falls back for null or undefined, so it returns 0.

quiz.question: Which line updates a React-style state object immutably, adding a tag to its tags array?
quiz.explanation: Only the first copies both the object and the nested array. The last one shares the original tags array, so push mutates old state.

quiz.question: Why can an arrow function be a poor choice for an object method that uses this?
options: Arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope, not from the object
Arrow functions cannot read outer variables
quiz.explanation: Arrows do not bind their own this, so inside an object literal this refers to the outer scope rather than the object.

quiz.question: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return?
quiz.explanation: Without a comparator, sort converts items to strings: '1' < '10' < '9'. Use sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers.

lesson.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: Event Loop, Promises and async/await
objectives: Explain how a single-threaded JavaScript runtime handles slow I/O without blocking.
Describe the call stack, the microtask queue and the task (macrotask) queue, and the order they run in.
Use promises and async/await, including proper error handling with try/catch.
Predict the output order of code mixing synchronous logs, promises and timers.
Recognise common async bugs such as missing await and accidental sequential requests.
lesson.definition: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, so long operations such as network requests, timers and file reads are handed to the environment (the browser or Node.js) and their results come back later as queued callbacks. The event loop runs those callbacks when the call stack is empty. A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, and async/await is syntax that lets you write promise-based code in a readable, top-to-bottom style.

theory.heading: Why asynchronous code exists
theory.body: If JavaScript waited synchronously for a 3-second LLM response, the browser could not repaint or respond to clicks and a Node.js server could not serve any other request. Instead, the runtime starts the operation, keeps running other code, and calls your code back when the result is ready. This non-blocking model is why one Node.js process can handle thousands of concurrent connections that mostly wait on I/O.
points: I/O-bound work (network, disk, database) fits the async model well.
CPU-bound work (image processing, large loops) still blocks the thread; move it to a Worker or worker_threads.
await pauses only the current async function, not the whole program.

theory.heading: Call stack, microtasks and tasks
theory.body: The event loop repeats one cycle: run a task to completion, then run every microtask in the microtask queue (including microtasks added while draining), then let the browser render if needed, then take the next task. Promise callbacks (then, catch, finally, code after await) and queueMicrotask are microtasks. setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks and UI events are tasks. So a resolved promise's callback always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled at the same moment.
points: Synchronous code first, until the stack is empty.
Then all microtasks, in FIFO order.
Then one macrotask, followed again by all microtasks.
setTimeout(fn, 0) means 'as a later task', not 'immediately'.

theory.heading: Promises
theory.body: A promise is pending, then settles once as fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with a reason); after settling it never changes. then returns a new promise, which is what makes chaining work: whatever a then callback returns becomes the next value, and a thrown error skips to the nearest catch. Always return or await promises you create; a promise that is created but not awaited can fail silently as an unhandled rejection.
points: new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...) wraps callback-style APIs.
Promise.resolve(v) and Promise.reject(e) create settled promises.
finally runs on both outcomes, useful for hiding a loading spinner.

theory.heading: async/await and error handling
theory.body: An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await pauses until the awaited promise settles, then resumes with its value or throws its rejection reason, so ordinary try/catch works. A frequent performance bug is awaiting independent requests one after another; start them together and await Promise.all instead. A frequent correctness bug is forgetting await, which returns a pending promise and lets errors escape your try/catch.
points: Sequential: const a = await getA(); const b = await getB(); takes timeA + timeB.
Parallel: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]); takes max(timeA, timeB).
fetch only rejects on network failure; check res.ok for 4xx/5xx.

example.title: Fetching a chat reply with proper error handling
example.body: This helper awaits the response, converts HTTP error statuses into thrown errors (fetch does not do that by itself) and always clears the loading state in finally.

demonstration.description: Predict the order before running. Synchronous logs come first, then the microtask from the promise, then the timer task.
demonstration.output:
1: script start
2: inside async, before await
2b: script end
3: promise
3b: after await
4: timeout

takeaways: JavaScript is single-threaded; the event loop runs queued callbacks when the stack is empty.
Microtasks (promise callbacks, code after await) run before the next macrotask (timers, I/O, events).
An async function always returns a promise; await unwraps it or throws its rejection.
Use Promise.all for independent requests instead of sequential awaits.
fetch resolves on HTTP errors; check res.ok yourself.
CPU-heavy work blocks the event loop; offload it.

interview.question: Explain the event loop.
interview.answer: JavaScript executes code on one call stack. Async operations are handled by the runtime, and their callbacks are queued. When the stack is empty, the event loop runs all pending microtasks (promise reactions), then takes the next macrotask (timer, I/O, UI event), runs it, drains microtasks again, and repeats.
interview.explanation: The key detail interviewers check is the microtask-before-macrotask rule. A small example (promise logs before setTimeout 0) makes the answer convincing.

interview.question: What is the difference between a promise and a callback?
interview.answer: A callback is a function you pass to be called later; nesting many leads to 'callback hell' and inconsistent error handling. A promise is an object representing a future result that settles once, can be chained, composes with Promise.all, and propagates errors to a single catch.
interview.explanation: Mention the trust guarantees: a promise settles only once, and its callbacks always run asynchronously.

interview.question: What does async/await do under the hood?
interview.answer: An async function returns a promise. Each await suspends the function and schedules its continuation as a microtask once the awaited promise settles; the result is returned or the rejection is thrown at the await point. It is syntax over promises, not a new threading model.
interview.explanation: Say clearly that await does not block the thread: other code keeps running while the function is suspended.

interview.question: Your page makes three independent API calls with three awaits in a row and feels slow. What would you change?
interview.answer: Start all three requests first and await them together with Promise.all, so total time is the slowest call rather than the sum. If one failure should not cancel the others, use Promise.allSettled and handle each result.
interview.explanation: This is a very common practical question. Mentioning allSettled for partial failure shows depth.

interview.question: Why might a try/catch around an async call not catch an error?
interview.answer: If the promise is not awaited (or returned) inside the try block, the function continues and the try block exits before the rejection happens, so the rejection becomes unhandled. Also, fetch does not reject on 404 or 500, so there is nothing to catch unless you check res.ok and throw.
interview.explanation: Covering both the missing-await bug and the fetch status behaviour shows real debugging experience.

practice.title: Simulate the event loop
practice.objective: Apply the event-loop rules (synchronous first, then all microtasks, then one macrotask at a time) to predict execution order.
practice.statement: Each input line is a statement in a script: '<type> <label>' or '<type> <label> then <type> <label>'. The type is sync, micro or macro. Processing a statement means: sync runs immediately, micro is added to the microtask queue, macro is added to the macrotask queue. When a task runs it prints its label; if it has a 'then' part, that child statement is processed at that moment. After the whole script, drain the microtask queue completely (including microtasks added while draining), then repeatedly run one macrotask followed by draining microtasks, until both queues are empty. Print labels in the order they run.
practice.input_format: One statement per line. Labels contain no spaces.
practice.output_format: One label per line in execution order.

example.input:
sync start
macro timeout
micro promise
sync end

constraints: At most one 'then' per line (children have no further children).
explanation: Parse each line into a task object; the part after ' then ' becomes a child task.
dispatch runs sync tasks immediately and pushes micro and macro tasks onto FIFO queues.
run records the label and dispatches the child, so a microtask can schedule a macrotask and vice versa.
After the script, drain microtasks fully; the while loop also picks up microtasks added during draining.
Then run exactly one macrotask at a time, draining microtasks after each, which mirrors the real event loop.

quiz.question: In what order are the letters logged?
quiz.explanation: Synchronous logs A and D run first, then the promise microtask C, then the timer task B.

quiz.question: What does an async function return when you call it?
options: The value of its return statement, synchronously
quiz.explanation: An async function always returns a promise that resolves with the returned value or rejects with the thrown error.

quiz.question: A page awaits getProfile(), then getCourses(), then getNotifications(). Each takes about 300 ms and none depends on another. What is the best improvement?
options: Start all three and await Promise.all
Call them inside a for loop with await
Use var instead of const for the results
quiz.explanation: Independent requests should run concurrently; Promise.all reduces total time from about 900 ms to about 300 ms.

quiz.question: A promise's executor calls resolve('ok') and then reject(new Error('x')). What is the promise's final state?
quiz.explanation: A promise settles only once. The first call wins; the later reject is ignored.

quiz.question: What is printed?
quiz.explanation: The async function runs synchronously until the first await, so 1 prints first. The rest is a microtask, so 3 prints before 2.

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
questions.answer: The browser parses the URL, resolves the domain through DNS, opens a TCP (or QUIC) connection, performs a TLS handshake for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, then parses HTML, fetches sub-resources (CSS, JS, images) and renders the page.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want the ordered chain, not every detail. Mention caching at each layer (DNS cache, HTTP cache) and that rendering involves the DOM and CSSOM for extra credit.

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: What is the difference between GET and POST?
questions.answer: GET retrieves a resource, is safe and idempotent, sends parameters in the URL and can be cached and bookmarked. POST submits data in the body to create something or trigger an action; it is neither safe nor idempotent and is not cached by default.
questions.explanation: Avoid saying POST is 'more secure': both are visible to anyone without HTTPS. The real difference is semantics, idempotency and caching.

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
questions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the request is not authenticated: credentials are missing or invalid. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you lack permission for this resource.
questions.explanation: A strong answer adds the UI consequence: on 401 redirect to login or refresh the token; on 403 show an access-denied message, because logging in again will not help.

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter for an API that calls an LLM?
questions.answer: An idempotent operation produces the same server state whether it runs once or many times. LLM calls are usually POSTs that cost money and may create records, so blind retries can double charges or duplicate messages. Use idempotency keys or deduplicate on the server before retrying.
questions.explanation: Linking HTTP semantics to cost and duplicate data shows you think about production behaviour, not just definitions.

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do web apps keep users logged in?
questions.answer: Each request is independent and the server keeps no built-in memory of earlier requests. Apps carry state explicitly: a session ID in a cookie that maps to server-side data, or a signed token (such as a JWT) sent on every request.
questions.explanation: Mention that statelessness is what allows horizontal scaling behind a load balancer, which leads naturally into session storage choices (Day 14).

questions.topic: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
questions.question: What changed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
questions.answer: HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexes many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, with header compression. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, which removes TCP head-of-line blocking and makes connection setup faster, especially on mobile networks.
questions.explanation: You do not need protocol internals; showing why multiplexing helps pages with many assets is enough.

questions.topic: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.answer: var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined when hoisted. let and const are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until declared. const cannot be reassigned, though an object it holds can still be mutated.
questions.explanation: Mention the loop example (var shares one variable across iterations) and that const is about the binding, not deep immutability.

questions.topic: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
questions.question: What is a closure? Give a practical example.
questions.answer: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created. Example: a counter factory that returns increment and get functions sharing a private count, or a debounce function that remembers its timer ID between calls.
questions.explanation: A concrete use (private state, debounce, React hooks) is what separates a strong answer from a memorised definition.

questions.topic: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
questions.question: What does this print, and why? for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));
questions.answer: It prints 3, 3, 3. var creates one function-scoped i shared by all callbacks, and the callbacks run after the loop has finished. Changing var to let prints 0, 1, 2 because let creates a new binding per iteration.
questions.explanation: This classic question tests scope, closures and the event loop together. Explain both the cause and the fix.

questions.topic: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
questions.question: When would you use reduce instead of map or filter?
questions.answer: Use reduce when the result has a different shape from the input, for example a total, an object keyed by category, or a lookup map. Use map for one-to-one transforms and filter for selecting items, because they are clearer.
questions.explanation: Interviewers like hearing that readability matters: chaining filter then map is often clearer than one clever reduce.

questions.topic: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
questions.question: Is the spread operator a deep copy? Why does this matter in React?
questions.answer: No. Spread copies only the top level; nested objects and arrays are shared references. In React, mutating a nested object after spreading changes the old state too, which can cause missed re-renders or bugs. Copy every level you change, or use structuredClone or a helper like Immer.
questions.explanation: Connecting shallow copies to React's reference-equality checks shows you understand why immutability matters, not just the rule.

days.title: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
days.focus: The web is a client-server system: a client such as a browser sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server returns an HTTP response. HTTP is a stateless, text-based application protocol (binary-framed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) that runs over TCP or QUIC, usually wrapped in TLS as HTTPS. DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the IP address the client connects to.
objectives: Explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a rendered page.
Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response: method, path, headers, body and status code.
Distinguish safe and idempotent HTTP methods and explain why the difference matters for retries.
Group status codes into their five classes and choose the right one for common situations.
Parse a raw HTTP request in JavaScript.
days.assignment: The input is a raw HTTP/1.1 request: a request line, header lines until a blank line, and an optional body. Print the method, the path without the query string, the decoded query parameters, the Host header and whether the method is safe and idempotent. Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent methods: the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: DNS resolves the name, TCP/QUIC connects, TLS secures, HTTP exchanges the request and response.
A request is method + target + headers + optional body; a response is status + headers + body.
Safe methods do not change state; idempotent methods can be repeated with the same effect.
POST is not idempotent, so retries need an idempotency key or server-side deduplication.
4xx means the client must change something; 5xx means the server failed and a retry may succeed.
HTTP is stateless; cookies and tokens carry identity between requests.

days.title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
days.focus: ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) and later versions added block-scoped variables, arrow functions, classes, modules, destructuring, spread syntax, promises and many array and object helpers to JavaScript. A closure is a function bundled with the variables of the scope it was created in, so it can read and update those variables even after the outer function has returned.
objectives: Explain the differences between var, let and const, including hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
Define a closure and use one to keep private state.
Use destructuring, spread/rest, template literals, optional chaining and nullish coalescing correctly.
Transform data with map, filter, reduce and sort without mutating the source.
Explain how arrow functions treat this differently from regular functions.
days.assignment: Each input line is 'name,course,score'. A record is valid when name and course are non-empty and score is a number from 0 to 100. Group valid records by course and, for each course in alphabetical order, print the average score (one decimal place), the top student (highest score; ties go to the alphabetically first name) and the number of students. Finally print how many lines were skipped as invalid. If there are no valid records, print 'No valid records' before the skipped count.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Prefer const, use let for reassignment, avoid var.
A closure keeps access to its outer variables; it enables private state and is behind React hooks.
?? falls back only for null/undefined; || also replaces 0, '' and false.
map, filter and reduce return new values; sort and reverse mutate unless you copy first.
Spread makes shallow copies: nested objects are still shared.
Arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope.

days.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: Event Loop, Promises and async/await
days.focus: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, so long operations such as network requests, timers and file reads are handed to the environment (the browser or Node.js) and their results come back later as queued callbacks. The event loop runs those callbacks when the call stack is empty. A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, and async/await is syntax that lets you write promise-based code in a readable, top-to-bottom style.
objectives: Explain how a single-threaded JavaScript runtime handles slow I/O without blocking.
Describe the call stack, the microtask queue and the task (macrotask) queue, and the order they run in.
Use promises and async/await, including proper error handling with try/catch.
Predict the output order of code mixing synchronous logs, promises and timers.
Recognise common async bugs such as missing await and accidental sequential requests.
